claims.title: Unverified public dependencies can gain the build runner's deployment authority
claims.description: An attacker who controls content served for a dependency named by the lockfile at `entity:public-package-registry` starts outside the build environment and can supply a malicious package on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`. The build runner accepts downloaded packages without signature verification. If the dependency resolution or image-build tooling executes package-provided lifecycle or build logic, that logic executes as `process:build-runner` and inherits its shared build token. It can then use `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` to designate an attacker-controlled image as the release. Second-order, the release is pushed through `flow:build-runner-to-image-registry:push-image`; every `process:store-server` obtains the selected image through `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` and restarts it, extending the external package supplier's authority into the till-container context across the store estate. This is conditional on the unverified `technology` of `process:build-runner` permitting dependency-supplied logic to execute during resolution or image creation.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.
We run about 1,200 stores.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `technology` on `process:build-runner`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:process:build-runner:technology`: an attacker must control a resolved package or registry response, but the package flow crosses to `boundary:internet` and has stated-absent package authentication in `absent:flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies:authentication`. Impact is high because `process:build-runner` holds credentials and can set the release through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, after which the image reaches the approximately 1,200 `process:store-server` instances, which are tagged `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Verify and pin dependency provenance before building
mitigations.detail: Require signature or attestation verification for packages retrieved on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, enforce immutable content digests from the lockfile, and fail the build when the expected publisher or artifact digest cannot be verified.

mitigations.summary: Isolate untrusted build logic from deployment authority
mitigations.detail: Run dependency resolution and package build scripts in a sandboxed workload without the build token; give only a separately controlled promotion step the narrowly scoped, short-lived authority needed on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`.

mitigations.summary: Require independently verified release artifacts at deployment
mitigations.detail: Have `process:store-server` accept only images signed by a trusted release-promotion identity, so an image produced after a compromised build step cannot become executable across the store estate.

claims.title: Shared build token may be intercepted between the build environment and deploy controller
claims.description: `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` crosses from the separate build environment to the corporate network and has unverified `encryption_in_transit`. The flow authenticates the call with the shared, never-rotated build token. If transport protection is absent, an attacker able to observe this inter-zone path can intercept that credential while `process:build-runner` sets the release on `process:deploy-controller`. The disclosed token enables subsequent use of the controller's current-release path; every `process:store-server` polls that controller and then pulls the selected image, so one recovered credential can reach the release mechanism for the whole estate. This is conditional on the unknown transport-encryption value, not a claim that the channel is plaintext.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release:encryption_in_transit`: an attacker needs an on-path position, but the flow crosses the build-environment/corporate-network boundary and exposes a long-lived shared credential if unencrypted. Impact is high because the intercepted credential governs the release record at `process:deploy-controller`, which is polled by every `process:store-server` in the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Protect and mutually authenticate the controller call
mitigations.detail: Set `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` to TLS 1.2+ with mTLS, preventing passive recovery of the token and verifying both service peers.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared static build token
mitigations.detail: Issue a distinct short-lived workload credential to each pipeline, scope it only to its permitted release operation, and rotate the existing token immediately.

claims.title: A pipeline operator can deny selecting the estate-wide release because the deploy credential is shared
claims.description: An operator of any pipeline holding the credential on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` can set the current release in `process:deploy-controller` and later deny having done so. The flow crosses from `boundary:build-environment` to `boundary:corporate-network`, but its shared build token identifies only the population of pipelines, not the individual pipeline or operator responsible for the release-selection action. Any controller-side evidence based on that credential can narrow the action only to that population. Second-order: `process:store-server` instances poll the selected release and pull the corresponding image, so a disputed release selection affects the accountability of rollout activity across the store estate.

grounds.text: a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: exploiting the evidentiary gap requires control of a pipeline or its shared token, but the shared credential is explicitly used across every pipeline and the release-setting flow crosses into `boundary:corporate-network`. Impact is high: `process:deploy-controller` selects the release consumed by the approximately 1,200-store `process:store-server` estate, whose assets include `business-critical-data` and `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared build token with per-pipeline identities
mitigations.detail: Give each pipeline a distinct, rotated credential on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` and record the verified pipeline identity and associated initiating principal with each release-selection request.

mitigations.summary: Create durable release-selection evidence
mitigations.detail: Have `process:deploy-controller` retain append-only security events containing the authenticated pipeline, originating developer or approval identity, image SHA, timestamp, outcome, and request identifier.

claims.title: An unreviewed manual rebuild may be deniable because developer authentication and audit evidence are undocumented
claims.description: A developer uses `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` to trigger an unreviewed rebuild of main in `process:build-runner`. That cross-boundary flow has `authentication: unknown`, and the model contains no `audit log` element or audit flow showing that the authenticated developer, rebuild request, source revision, and outcome are retained. If the unknown authentication does not provide an individual verified identity and durable audit record, a developer can deny initiating the rebuild after its image is pushed and selected for deployment. Second-order: the rebuild feeds `flow:build-runner-to-image-registry:push-image` and can result in a release selected through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, leaving the later store-estate rollout without conclusive evidence of who initiated it. This is conditional on the undocumented authentication and record handling, not an assertion that no logging exists in deployment.

grounds.text: any developer can log in to the build runner and kick off a rebuild of `main` by hand; that path does not require a merge and is not reviewed

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `authentication` on `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown authentication state: the action requires a developer login, but every developer is permitted to initiate the unreviewed rebuild and the login flow crosses from `boundary:corporate-network` into `boundary:build-environment`. Impact is high: `process:build-runner` holds `credentials` and `business-critical-data`, and its output can be selected for rollout to `process:store-server`, which is `availability-critical` across the store estate.

mitigations.summary: Verify and retain individual developer identity for manual rebuilds
mitigations.detail: Require individual non-shared authentication on `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` and emit structured, tamper-resistant events recording the verified subject, requested revision, rebuild identifier, timestamp, and result.

mitigations.summary: Make manual rebuilds traceable through deployment
mitigations.detail: Propagate the initiating developer and rebuild identifier into image metadata and release-selection records, while retaining the build-runner identity separately, so later deployment evidence can link a rollout to its human initiator.

claims.title: Shared build token lets an attacker impersonate the build runner to release an image
claims.description: An attacker who obtains the shared build token can impersonate `process:build-runner` on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` and instruct `process:deploy-controller` to make an attacker-chosen image SHA the current release. The token is the same for every pipeline and has never been rotated, so its possession is sufficient to present the shared pipeline identity rather than an attributable workload identity. Second-order: `process:store-server` polls the controller and pulls the selected image from `store:image-registry`, so the impersonation can direct rollout across the approximately 1,200-store estate.

grounds.text: The token the runner uses to call the controller is a shared build token that is the same for every pipeline and has not been rotated since the pipeline was set up.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: exploitation requires obtaining the shared token, but it is long-lived, shared by every pipeline, and the flow crosses from `boundary:build-environment` to `boundary:corporate-network` (`crossing:flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`). Impact is high: `process:deploy-controller` selects the estate release, while `process:store-server` represents about 1,200 servers and is tagged `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Replace the shared build token with per-workload identity
mitigations.detail: Use a distinct workload identity or mTLS certificate for each pipeline on `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, rather than a token shared by all pipelines.

mitigations.summary: Use short-lived, audience-bound deployment credentials
mitigations.detail: Issue short-lived credentials restricted to `process:deploy-controller`, rotate any remaining static secret, and record the originating pipeline identity for each release update.

claims.title: Unverified package provenance lets an attacker impersonate a trusted dependency source
claims.description: On `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, `process:build-runner` does not verify signatures on downloaded packages. An attacker able to impersonate or interfere with the public dependency source can supply a package that the runner accepts as the lockfile-selected dependency, rather than as attacker-supplied content. The flow also has unknown transport protection, so server authentication is not established by the model. Second-order: the dependency is incorporated into the image pushed to `store:image-registry`; the build runner then sets the release through `process:deploy-controller`, reaching the store-server fleet.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: this is a boundary crossing to `boundary:internet` with package-signature verification stated absent (`absent:flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies:authentication`), although successful source impersonation may require an on-path, DNS, or dependency-source compromise; transport protection is also unverified. Impact is high: accepted dependencies are built into images that ultimately deploy to `process:store-server`, whose fleet is tagged `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Verify signed dependency provenance before building
mitigations.detail: Require signature verification against trusted publisher keys for every package on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, and reject unsigned or untrusted artifacts.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate the registry endpoint
mitigations.detail: Use TLS with full certificate-chain validation for the public registry connection and constrain trusted package sources and publisher identities.

If the undocumented login does not strongly verify the human and server identities, an attacker with a corporate-network foothold could impersonate `entity:developer` to `process:build-runner` and start the unreviewed manual rebuild. Second-order: the build runner holds the credential used to update `process:deploy-controller`, and its normal build path pushes images to `store:image-registry`, making the build environment a route to releases consumed by the store estate. claims.title: Store release polling can be modified in transit to redirect deployments
claims.description: If the unknown transport protection on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release` does not provide authenticated integrity for the controller response, an attacker on the retail WAN can alter the returned current-release image SHA before it reaches `process:store-server`. The store server may then treat the substituted SHA as the estate release and retrieve a different image from `store:image-registry`. This is conditional on the unknown `encryption_in_transit`, protocol, and authentication attributes; it does not assert that the retail-WAN connection is unprotected.

grounds.text: Every store server asks the deploy controller once a minute what the current release is, and if it differs from what it is running it pulls that image from the registry and restarts the container.
Traffic between the stores and the corporate network goes over the retail WAN.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, `authentication` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, `protocol` on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown controls for boundary-crossing `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release`; an attacker must obtain a position on the retail WAN. Impact is high because a forged release selection can cause `process:store-server`, representing approximately 1,200 servers, to restart into a substituted deployment.

mitigations.summary: Mutually authenticate and integrity-protect release polling
mitigations.detail: Use mTLS on `flow:store-server-to-deploy-controller:poll-current-release` and ensure the controller response is protected end to end.

mitigations.summary: Sign and verify release manifests
mitigations.detail: Have `process:deploy-controller` sign the release manifest and require each `process:store-server` to verify the signature and authorized image digest before pulling or restarting.

claims.title: Container images can be altered in transit while stores pull them over the WAN
claims.description: If `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` lacks authenticated transport integrity, an attacker positioned on the WAN path between `boundary:store-estate` and `boundary:build-environment` can alter the container image bytes delivered to `process:store-server`. A store that accepts the altered image restarts and executes attacker-controlled till-software code. The same opportunity can affect each store's pull path, extending the integrity loss across the modeled fleet. This threat is conditional on the currently unknown transport, protocol, and authentication attributes for the image-pull flow.

grounds.text: The image registry is reachable from the store estate over the WAN.
if it differs from what it is running it pulls that image from the registry and restarts the container.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, `authentication` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, `protocol` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on the unknown protections of the boundary-crossing image-pull flow; the attacker needs a WAN on-path position. Impact is high because altered container code is executed by `process:store-server`, which represents about 1,200 availability-critical store servers.

mitigations.summary: Protect registry pulls with authenticated TLS
mitigations.detail: Configure `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` for TLS with registry identity verification and mutually authenticated store identities.

mitigations.summary: Require image signature and digest verification at each store
mitigations.detail: Require `process:store-server` to verify a trusted image signature and immutable content digest before starting an image, independently of transport protection.

claims.title: Repeated manual rebuilds can exhaust the shared build runner
claims.description: A malicious or compromised `entity:developer` on `boundary:corporate-network` can repeatedly invoke `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild` across the boundary into `process:build-runner`. Each invocation performs source fetching, dependency resolution, image production, and image publication, so the attacker spends only repeated rebuild requests while consuming the runner's finite CPU, memory, worker, network, and dependency-resolution capacity. Whether authentication-specific rate limits, concurrent-build limits, queuing bounds, and cancellation controls exist on this flow is unknown. Second-order, exhaustion of `process:build-runner` delays legitimate builds and the update path through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release` and `flow:build-runner-to-image-registry:push-image`, preventing timely fixes and releases to `process:store-server` across the estate.

grounds.text: any developer can log in to the build runner and kick off a rebuild of `main` by hand; that path does not require a merge and is not reviewed.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `authentication` on `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: any `entity:developer` can access the boundary-crossing `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, but the attacker needs an internal developer account or its compromise; the flow's authentication details are `unknown`. Impact is medium: `process:build-runner` carries `business-critical-data`, and its exhaustion blocks the build-and-release path needed to update the store fleet, but the model does not establish that currently running tills immediately stop.

mitigations.summary: Bound and meter manual rebuild requests
mitigations.detail: Require an approved trigger for `flow:developer-to-build-runner:manual-rebuild`, enforce per-developer rate and concurrent-build limits, and reject or coalesce duplicate builds of the same `main` revision before expensive work starts.

mitigations.summary: Isolate and shed build workload
mitigations.detail: Set bounded build-worker, CPU, memory, disk, network, and dependency-download budgets on `process:build-runner`; use cancellation and fail-fast queue limits so manual rebuild bursts cannot indefinitely delay legitimate releases.

claims.title: Unverified public dependency downloads can exhaust build-runner resources
claims.description: An attacker able to control or impersonate content from `entity:public-package-registry` can return an oversized or pathological dependency package over `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`. `process:build-runner` accepts downloaded packages without signature verification, so, if package-size, extraction, parse-complexity, timeout, and storage quotas are not enforced, one inexpensive hostile response can consume disproportionate runner bandwidth, disk, CPU, or memory and crash or stall builds. Second-order, a stalled `process:build-runner` cannot publish images through `flow:build-runner-to-image-registry:push-image` or set releases through `flow:build-runner-to-deploy-controller:set-current-release`, delaying updates to `process:store-server`.

grounds.text: the lockfile is taken as given — the runner does not verify signatures on what it downloads.

verdict.reason: The model establishes that package signatures are not verified, but it does not state whether package-size limits, extraction and parsing limits, timeouts, or resource quotas prevent a hostile dependency response from exhausting the build runner.

related_unknowns.subject: Are package-size, extraction, parsing, timeout, storage, CPU, and memory limits enforced for dependencies downloaded by the build runner?

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium when the undocumented resource controls are treated as absent: an attacker who controls a dependency artifact delivered over the internet-facing public-registry flow can supply a pathological package, though control of a selected dependency remains a prerequisite. Impact is medium because exhausting `process:build-runner` blocks image publication and release selection, delaying updates to the store estate, while the model does not establish interruption of already-running tills.

mitigations.summary: Verify and constrain dependency artifacts before build processing
mitigations.detail: Require authenticated signature or provenance verification for artifacts on `flow:build-runner-to-public-package-registry:resolve-dependencies`, pin trusted registries or mirrors, and reject artifacts that fail verification before extraction or build execution.

mitigations.summary: Apply dependency download and extraction resource limits
mitigations.detail: Enforce per-artifact and total download-size caps, decompression-ratio and archive-entry limits, parse timeouts, and isolated CPU, memory, disk, and network quotas for dependency resolution in `process:build-runner`.

claims.title: Source code may be readable on the unverified build-runner-to-git-server link
claims.description: `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source` carries the merged source commit across the build-environment/corporate-network boundary, but its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If that attribute resolves to no effective transport encryption, a network observer on this path can intercept the application's source code while `process:build-runner` reads it from `store:git-server`. The disclosed source can reveal implementation details and vulnerabilities that help an attacker target the later build and deployment path, including image production and release selection. This finding is conditional on the unverified transport control.

grounds.text: The build runner picks the merge up, fetches the source, resolves the dependency lockfile and produces a container image.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source:encryption_in_transit`: interception requires access to an inter-zone path, but the path is a documented boundary crossing. Impact is medium because the flow and `store:git-server` contain business-critical source code, whose disclosure assists attacks on the software and build pipeline.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt the source-fetch hop
mitigations.detail: Require TLS 1.2+ for `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source`, preferably with mTLS between the build runner and git server.

mitigations.summary: Restrict source-read credentials
mitigations.detail: Use a narrowly scoped runner identity that can read only the required repository and commit, reducing exposure if a client identity is compromised.

claims.title: Container images may be intercepted while stores pull them over the WAN
claims.description: `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` transfers the current container image from `store:image-registry` to `process:store-server` across the store-estate/build-environment boundary, and its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If the WAN pull lacks effective encryption, an attacker with an observation position on the retail WAN can intercept image layers and inspect the till software used throughout the store estate. The image contents can expose operational implementation details that enable more targeted attacks against the running store-server software; the exposure applies repeatedly as stores update. This is conditional on verifying that the unknown transport-encryption attribute is not protective.

grounds.text: The image registry is reachable from the store estate over the WAN. Traffic between the stores and the corporate network goes over the retail WAN.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_in_transit` on `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image:encryption_in_transit`: an attacker must observe the retail-WAN boundary crossing, but every store retrieves images over that path. Impact is medium because the images are tagged business-critical data and disclose the software deployed across the roughly 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Require encrypted registry pulls from every store
mitigations.detail: Configure `flow:store-server-to-image-registry:pull-image` for TLS 1.2+ and authenticate the registry endpoint; use mTLS where store identities can be managed.

mitigations.summary: Minimize sensitive image contents
mitigations.detail: Keep credentials, tokens, and environment-specific configuration out of container layers, and obtain them at runtime from a dedicated secret-management mechanism.

claims.title: Git source may be exposed from operational copies if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:git-server` holds developer branches and main, while its `encryption_at_rest` and data classification are unknown. If the unverified encryption attribute resolves to unencrypted storage, an attacker or over-privileged operator who obtains a server volume, backup, snapshot, or decommissioned storage copy can read the repository contents directly without using `flow:build-runner-to-git-server:fetch-source`. The source disclosure supplies implementation detail that can be used to target `process:build-runner` and the downstream image and release pipeline. This is conditional on `store:git-server` lacking effective at-rest encryption; it does not assert that it is currently unencrypted.

grounds.text: Nobody has documented whether the git server encrypts what it stores

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_at_rest` on `store:git-server`, `data_classification` on `store:git-server`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:store:git-server:encryption_at_rest`: obtaining an operational storage copy requires storage-layer or operational access, but no verified encryption control is recorded. Impact is medium because `store:git-server` holds business-critical source code that can reveal implementation details relevant to the build and deployment path.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce encryption for repository storage and copies
mitigations.detail: Establish the at-rest posture of `store:git-server`, then require KMS-managed encryption for its primary volumes, backups, snapshots, and replicas; limit export and restore permissions.

mitigations.summary: Protect repository backup access separately
mitigations.detail: Apply deny-by-default access controls and distinct least-privilege principals to backup and snapshot operations rather than relying on git-server application access controls.

claims.title: Registry images may be exposed from operational copies if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:image-registry` stores built container images used by the store fleet, but its `encryption_at_rest` and data classification are unknown. If this unresolved encryption state means images are stored without effective at-rest protection, a person who accesses an exported image-store volume, backup, snapshot, or decommissioned media can read image layers outside the registry's normal pull path. This exposes business-critical till-software implementation details and can enable more focused attacks against `process:store-server` when it runs those images across the estate. The threat is conditional on the unknown at-rest control and does not claim the registry is unencrypted.

grounds.text: Nobody has documented whether the git server encrypts what it stores, or whether the image registry does.

verdict.reason: The claim rests on `encryption_at_rest` on `store:image-registry`, `data_classification` on `store:image-registry`, which the input never stated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional on `unknown:store:image-registry:encryption_at_rest`: storage-layer access is required, but the model records no verified encryption for the registry. Impact is medium because `store:image-registry` contains business-critical container images deployed to the approximately 1,200-store estate.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt registry storage and every operational copy
mitigations.detail: Determine the actual protection for `store:image-registry`, then enforce managed-key encryption on image blobs, backing volumes, backups, snapshots, and replicas.

mitigations.summary: Limit storage-layer readers and image exports
mitigations.detail: Use separate least-privilege principals for registry administration, backup, and restore, and audit bulk image export or snapshot retrieval.
